questionText: How do transient, scoped, and singleton lifetimes behave in Microsoft.Extensions.DependencyInjection?
shortAnswer: Transient = new instance every resolution; scoped = one per scope (per HTTP request); singleton = one for the app lifetime. Mismatches (scoped-in-singleton) cause captive dependencies — the container can validate scopes in development.
detailedAnswer: Transient (AddTransient): fresh instance per injection — stateless services, mappers, validators. Scoped (AddScoped): one instance per IServiceScope — DbContext, unit-of-work, request state (HTTP creates a scope per request automatically; background code must CreateScope explicitly!). Singleton (AddSingleton): one forever — configuration, caches, thread-safe registries (must be thread-safe!). Captive dependency: singleton holding a scoped service (the scoped instance lives as long as the singleton — DbContext held for the app lifetime: stale data + concurrency exceptions + leak). Prevention: ValidateScopes in Development (throws on captive capture at resolution — our templates should enable it), architecture (singletons depend only on singletons + factories: IServiceScopeFactory/Func<T> for on-demand scoped work). Disposal: container disposesACGG scoped/transient IDisposables it creates at scope end (another reason scopes matter). TryAdd variants (TryAddScoped — register only if absent: library defaults overridable), Replace/Remove for tests. Keyed services (.NET 8+: AddKeyedSingleton("a", ...), [FromKeyedServices("a")] — multiple implementations without factory boilerplate).
internalWorking: Scopes are dictionaries (resolved-service cache per scope); singletons live in the root provider (never disposed until host shutdown). ValidateScopes wraps resolutions with scope-ownership checks (dev-only cost). Keyed services add a parallel keyed registry resolved via KeyedService.AnyKey plumbing.
realWorldUsage: DbContext per request, caches as singletons, validators transient, multi-provider strategies via keyed services.
commonMistake: Scoped-in-singleton (the #1 DI production bug), no scope in background workers (InvalidOperationException: cannot resolve scoped from root), and transient IDisposables resolved from root (leak until host ends — resolve from scopes).
technicalConversation: Ask how their background workers get a DbContext — CreateScope per unit of work is the answer; anything else is the bug.
interviewFollowUp: Why does the container dispose scoped services but (almost) never transient ones from the root?
keyTakeaway: Transient = always new, scoped = per request/scope, singleton = forever. Singletons take factories, not scoped services.

questionText: What is a captive dependency, how do you detect it, and how do you fix each variant?
shortAnswer: A captive dependency is a short-lived service held by a longer-lived one (scoped DbContext in a singleton), living past its intended lifetime. Detect with ValidateScopes/ValidateOnBuild in dev + code review of singleton ctors; fix with factories (IServiceScopeFactory, Func<T>) or lifetime realignment.
detailedAnswer: Variants: (1) Singleton → scoped (classic: cache holds DbContext — stale tracked entities, concurrency exceptions under load, memory growth). Fix: inject IServiceScopeFactory, create a scope per operation. (2) Singleton → transient IDisposable (container tracks it to root disposal — effectively singleton lifetime + delayed cleanup; fix: factory or scope). (3) Scoped → transient stateful (shorter-than-expected sharing within a request — usually intended, but surprising for 'per-operation' assumptions; fix: explicit scopes per operation). (4) Captured scope: BackgroundService resolving scoped at startup (root scope held forever — same disease; fix: scope per iteration). Detection: options.ValidateScopes = true + ValidateOnBuild in Development (throws InvalidOperationException naming the chain at startup/first resolve — enable always in dev/test!); production safety comes from review (singleton ctors audited for non-singleton params) + tests resolving the full graph (GetRequiredService for every registration in a test host boots captive chains). Our projects: Api Program should enable validation in Development (cheap, catches the class early).
internalWorking: ValidateScopes tags each resolved service with its owning scope; injecting a scoped-tagged instance into singleton construction throws (the container tracks provenance). ValidateOnBuild resolves every registration at host build (fail fast on missing deps + open generics + captive chains reachable at build).
realWorldUsage: Singleton caches, background workers, hosted services, SignalR hubs (scoped per connection — same rules), and test hosts.
commonMistake: Validation only in prod-debugging (enable in dev always), 'fixing' by making everything singleton (DbContext singleton = concurrency disaster), and factory-per-call without scope disposal (leak — using scope).
technicalConversation: Ask them to audit one singleton's constructor right now — every non-singleton parameter is a suspect until proven factory.
interviewFollowUp: Why is making the DbContext singleton worse than the captive dependency it 'fixes'?
keyTakeaway: Short-lived must never be held by long-lived. Validate in dev, factories in singletons, audit ctors.

questionText: What are keyed services in .NET 8+, and what problems do they solve?
shortAnswer: Keyed services register multiple implementations under keys (AddKeyedSingleton<IMailer>("smtp", ...)) and resolve via [FromKeyedServices("smtp")] — eliminating hand-written factories/strategy dictionaries for multi-provider scenarios (several payment gateways, notifiers, serializers).
detailedAnswer: Before: Dictionary<string, IPayment> built manually, or IEnumerable<IPayment> + switch (registration order fragile). Now: AddKeyedTransient<INotifier, EmailNotifier>("email"), AddKeyedTransient<INotifier, SmsNotifier>("sms"); consume [FromKeyedServices("email")] INotifier email (minimal APIs, controllers, ctors all support the attribute). Keys are object (strings, enums, types — enums recommended: NotifyChannel.Email). Resolve-all: GetKeyedServices<T>(key) / GetRequiredKeyedService. Patterns: per-tenant providers (key = tenant id), strategy by message type, A/B implementations, and test doubles swapped per key. Limits: keys must be known at registration (no runtime-computed key sets without custom factories — combine: keyed providers + a small router service for dynamic dispatch), attribute-only injection points (manual GetRequiredKeyedService in factories/workers), and options-per-key need named options alongside. Versus Scrutor/assemblies scanning: complementary (scan + key by convention). Testing: replace one key with a fake (services.RemoveAll + AddKeyedSingleton fake) — surgical, other keys untouched.
internalWorking: Keyed registry parallels the type registry (key+type compound lookup, same lifetime semantics — scoped keyed = per-scope per-key). FromKeyedServices generates keyed-resolution call sites at compile time (source-generated wiring, no runtime reflection per resolve).
realWorldUsage: Multi-channel notifiers, payment/shipping providers, tenant-specific adapters, serializer choices (JSON/XML), and per-region clients.
commonMistake: String keys with typos (use enums/constants), dynamic keys without a router (keyed needs static keys — add the router), and keyed + IEnumerable<T> confusion (unk keyed resolves all keyed? No — GetServices returns unkeyed only; use GetKeyedServices).
technicalConversation: Ask how many hand-written factory dictionaries they maintain — each is a keyed-services candidate, and the router covers the dynamic remainder.
interviewFollowUp: How do keyed services interact with IEnumerable<T> resolution, and what fills that gap?
keyTakeaway: Keyed services = multi-implementation without factory boilerplate. Enums for keys, router for dynamic choice.

questionText: How do TryAdd, Replace, and Remove help with library defaults and testing?
shortAnswer: TryAdd* registers only if absent (libraries ship overridable defaults); Replace swaps an implementation (tests, decorators); Remove drops registrations. Together they make composition explicit: defaults → overrides → test doubles, applied in order.
detailedAnswer: Library pattern: services.TryAddScoped<ICache, MemoryCache>() — app's own AddScoped<ICache, RedisCache> wins regardless of order (TryAdd never overwrites). TryAddEnumerable for multi-registration (adds only missing implementation-type pairs — options configurators, health checks). Replace (new ServiceDescriptor swap): services.Replace(ServiceDescriptor.Scoped<IClock, FakeClock>()) in tests — deterministic time without touching production code. Remove/RemoveAll: strip defaults before re-adding variants (RemoveAll<IHostedService> in tests to silence background workers!). Order discipline: defaults (libraries) → app registrations → environment/test overrides last. Decorators: manual (wrap descriptor: services.Replace(new Transient<IRepo>(sp => new CachedRepo(sp.GetRequiredService<ConcreteRepo>())))) or Scrutor's Decorate (cleaner). Verification: assert registration expectations in tests (provider.GetRequiredService resolves; fake is the instance type). Anti-patterns: Replace in production code paths (composition should be static — environment-specific Startup, not runtime swaps), and TryAdd for app code (hides duplicate-registration bugs — TryAdd is for libraries).
internalWorking: ServiceCollection is an ordered list of descriptors; last registration wins for single resolution (TryAdd checks existing first). Replace swaps in place (preserving order). The provider compiles the list once at build (ValidateOnBuild walks it).
realWorldUsage: Library authoring, test doubles (clocks, gateways, file systems), decorator chains, and silencing hosted services in tests.
commonMistake: Production Replace-by-environment (use Startup variants), TryAdd masking duplicate app registrations, and un-disposed replaced disposables (container owns registered instances — replaced ones still dispose if created... verify lifetime!).
technicalConversation: Ask how their tests swap time/external services — Replace/RemoveAll patterns versus statics reveal testability maturity.
interviewFollowUp: Why is TryAdd for libraries but plain Add for application code?
keyTakeaway: TryAdd = library defaults, Replace/Remove = test overrides, order = defaults→app→tests.

questionText: How do logging scopes and correlation IDs work across async operations?
shortAnswer: BeginScope pushes properties (CorrelationId) into an AsyncLocal stack — every log inside (across awaits) carries them. Middleware/generators assign one id per request; background jobs per operation. Sinks render scopes alongside events, enabling end-to-end tracing in queries.
detailedAnswer: Mechanics: using (logger.BeginScope("OrderId:{OrderId}", id)) — the scope dictionary flows through await (AsyncLocal) but NOT across explicit threads/Task.Run without ExecutionContext flow (suppressed contexts drop scopes — rare, know it). Request pattern: middleware generates/reads X-Correlation-Id (or TraceIdentifier), BeginScope for the pipeline, response echoes the header (clients correlate support tickets). Background: per-message/per-tick scope (job id + iteration). Serilog: enrichers (WithCorrelationId, machine/thread) + output template including {Properties} or JSON sinks (properties first-class). OTel: Activity.Current.TraceId supersedes manual ids (W3C traceparent across services — propagate via headers automatically with instrumentation). Costs: scope allocation per operation (tiny; pooled internally), property serialization per event (keep scopes small — ids, not payloads). Testing: in-memory sink asserting scope properties present. Pitfalls: scopes in long-lived singletons (leak/stale — scope per operation, dispose!), PII in scopes (user ids need policy — hash or omit), and scope loss across Task.Run + ConfigureAwait(false)... (ConfigureAwait(false) preserves ExecutionContext — scopes survive; SuppressFlow drops them).
internalWorking: Scopes live in AsyncLocal<Stack<...>> (ExecutionContext flow across awaits; zero cost when no scopes active). Sinks enumerate active scopes at event creation (copy-on-write snapshot). OTel Activities ride the same context (nested, W3C-propagated).
realWorldUsage: Request tracing, support-ticket correlation, batch-job run ids, and multi-service trace stitching.
commonMistake: No correlation at all (incident archaeology impossible), PII in scopes (leak by design), scopes surviving disposal (using discipline), and expecting scopes across process boundaries (propagate via headers/Activity).
technicalConversation: Ask how they trace one failing request across three services today — header-propagated ids (good), log timestamps (hope), or 'add more logs and retry' (debt).
interviewFollowUp: How do OpenTelemetry Activities relate to logging scopes, and which should carry the correlation id?
keyTakeaway: One scope per operation, ids not payloads, propagate across boundaries. Correlate everything.

questionText: How do you configure Serilog sinks, enrichment, and filtering for containers versus local dev?
shortAnswer: Dev: pretty console + rolling file + Seq (queryable). Containers: JSON console (collectors scrape stdout) + warning+ remote sink. Enrich with machine/thread/correlation; filter noisy categories per sink; never log PII/secrets — destructure policies keep payloads lean.
detailedAnswer: Dev setup: WriteTo.Console(theme) + File(rolling) + Seq(http://localhost:5341) for clickable structured queries. Container setup: console JSON formatter only (12-factor logs = stdout stream; files die with containers), level overrides (Microsoft.* Warning, System Warning, App Information), remote errors-only sink (AppInsights/Datadog) with batching + retry (sink failures must never crash the app — AuditTo vs WriteTo choice: audit sinks throw on failure, use for must-not-lose audit trails only). Enrichment: .Enrich.FromLogContext() (scopes!), WithMachineName/ThreadId/ProcessId, custom request-path enricher (endpoint tagging for dashboards). Filtering: .Filter.ByExcluding(Matching.FromSource("Microsoft.EntityFrameworkCore") && level < Warning) per-sink expressions; sub-loggers for split streams (errors → pager sink, all → archive). Destructuring: policies per type (ByTransforming<Order>), maximum depth caps (destructuring graphs → payload bombs), Stringify for odd types. Config: appsettings Serilog section (levels per environment — ours does this) with reload support; secrets in sink connection strings via Key Vault refs. Testing: Serilog.Sinks.InMemory/TestCorrelator asserting events (not text!).
codeExample:
Log.Logger = new LoggerConfiguration()
    .MinimumLevel.Information()
    .MinimumLevel.Override("Microsoft", LogEventLevel.Warning)
    .Enrich.FromLogContext()
    .Enrich.WithMachineName()
    .WriteTo.Console(new JsonFormatter())          // containers: JSON stdout
    .WriteTo.Seq("http://seq:5341", restrictedToMinimumLevel: LogEventLevel.Debug) // dev query
    .CreateLogger();
internalWorking: Pipeline: events → level check → enrichers (property injection) → filters → sinks (each async/batched independently; failures isolated per sink unless AuditTo). JSON formatter serializes properties (destructuring policies applied); text formatter renders templates. Reloadable level switches (LoggingLevelSwitch) allow runtime tuning without restart.
realWorldUsage: Container log collection, Seq-powered incident queries, audit trails, and per-tenant log routing.
commonMistake: File sinks in containers (lost on restart — stdout!), text format in collectors (unqueryable — JSON), PII in properties (index + leak), and AuditTo everywhere (sink outage crashes app — reserve for audit).
technicalConversation: Ask what their prod logs look like to a collector — JSON stdout (correct) versus files-in-container (lost) versus text blobs (unqueryable).
interviewFollowUp: What is the difference between WriteTo and AuditTo, and when is each correct?
keyTakeaway: JSON stdout in containers, Seq locally, enrich contextually, filter per sink, never PII.

questionText: How do you control log volume and cost in high-traffic production systems?
shortAnswer: Level ruthlessly (Information for business milestones, Warning+ for anomalies), sample verbose paths, aggregate counters instead of per-event logs, set retention/quotas, and alert on volume anomalies. Logging is a budget: every event has storage, ingestion, and attention cost.
detailedAnswer: Levers: (1) Levels per category (Microsoft.* Warning saves ~80% of framework chatter; EF commands off outside debugging). (2) Sampling: verbose paths log 1/N (deterministic sample keys — same request sampled across services via trace id modulo). (3) Aggregation: counters/histograms (Meter API) instead of per-request events (latency percentiles without a billion rows). (4) Scopes over repeats (correlation once per operation, not per line). (5) Retention/quotas (hot 7d, warm 30d, cold archive; per-service quotas with alerts at 80%). (6) Dynamic switches (LoggingLevelSwitch per namespace toggled at runtime for incidents — verbose for 10 minutes, then back). (7) Drop rules (health-check endpoints, static assets — filter at the sink, never in code paths that need them in incidents... keep access logs sampled separately). Cost math: events/sec × bytes × retention × ingestion price (cloud logging bills shock teams yearly — budget per service). Alerting on volume itself (5x spike = incident or loop-bug — faster than most error alerts). PII minimization doubles as cost control (smaller events). Reviews: log-volume line item in design reviews for hot paths.
internalWorking: Level switches are volatile reads (nanoseconds when off). Sampling by trace id keeps distributed traces coherent (all-or-nothing per trace — critical for usefulness). Meters aggregate in-process (no per-event allocation) exporting deltas on intervals.
realWorldUsage: High-RPS APIs, background fleet logging, multi-tenant platforms (per-tenant quotas), and cost-capped startups.
commonMistake: Debug in prod permanently (volume + cost), per-request Information storms (aggregate!), unsampled health checks (50% of volume is probes — filter), and alerting on log text (alert on metrics, investigate in logs).
technicalConversation: Ask what their logging bill is and what percent is health checks — the answers reveal whether volume is managed or accidental.
interviewFollowUp: Why sample by trace id rather than randomly per event?
keyTakeaway: Log by budget: levels, sampling, aggregates, retention. Volume anomalies are incidents too.

questionText: How do you test code that depends on the DI container (registrations, lifetimes, hosted services)?
shortAnswer: Test registrations (every service resolves), lifetimes (scoped isolation, captive chains via ValidateScopes), and hosted-service logic (extract from IHostedService into testable units). Use WebApplicationFactory/Test host with overridden doubles — never statics or real externals.
detailedAnswer: Layers: (1) Composition test: build the real host in tests, GetRequiredService for every key abstraction (fails on missing/transitive gaps — catches 90% of wiring bugs). (2) Lifetime tests: resolve scoped twice in one scope (same instance) vs two scopes (different); singleton stability; ValidateScopes on in dev/test (captive chains throw). (3) Override doubles: WebApplicationFactory.WithWebHostBuilder(ConfigureTestServices: RemoveAll + AddFake) — clocks, gateways, file systems, DbContext to test DB. (4) Hosted services: test the worker logic class directly (pure-ish ExecuteAsync with injected fakes + CancellationToken), and separately assert registration (StartAsync wiring smoke). (5) Options: Options.Create(fakes) for unit tests (no config files). (6) Keyed: resolve each key (missing-key typos fail here, not prod). Anti-patterns: new-ing the container per test without disposal (leak + slowness — fixture-shared host), testing Microsoft's container itself (test YOUR graph), and statics to dodge DI (untestable by construction). Our test project already follows this: real services + real repos over isolated SQLite (composition proven per test run).
internalWorking: Host.Build validates the descriptor graph (open generics, missing deps with ValidateOnBuild); scopes enforce lifetime boundaries at resolve time; test doubles swap descriptors before provider compilation (order: defaults → app → test overrides).
realWorldUsage: CI composition gates, lifetime regression tests, and WebApplicationFactory integration suites.
commonMistake: No composition test (wiring bugs reach staging), per-test hosts (slow suites — fixture sharing), and faking the container itself (test the graph, not the framework).
technicalConversation: Ask when their DI wiring last broke prod — missing transitive registration is the classic; composition tests are the vaccine.
interviewFollowUp: Why should tests resolve the real graph with faked leaves instead of mocking every service?
keyTakeaway: Resolve everything, isolate scopes, override leaves. Composition is testable infrastructure.

questionText: How does OpenTelemetry unify logs, metrics, and traces in .NET, and where do you start?
shortAnswer: OTel uses Activity (traces) + Meter (metrics) + ILogger bridge (logs) sharing one context (TraceId), exported via OTLP to any backend. Start: instrument ASP.NET + HttpClient + EF (built-in), propagate W3C headers, add a few custom Activities/Meters, export to one backend — then alert on metrics, investigate in traces, audit in logs.
detailedAnswer: Pieces: System.Diagnostics.Activity (spans — started automatically by ASP.NET/HttpClient/SqlClient instrumentation; custom via ActivitySource for domain operations), Meter/Histogram/Counter (app metrics — latency, totals, queue depth), ILogger (existing logs join traces via TraceId scope automatically with OTel logging). Context: W3C traceparent/tracestate headers propagate across HTTP/gRPC/queues (machine-to-machine continuity). Exporter: OTLP to Collector → Jaeger/Tempo (traces), Prometheus (metrics), Loki/Seq (logs) — one pipeline, swappable backends. Sampling: head-based probability (dev 100%, prod 1–10% + tail-based for errors — keep all errors, sample successes). Our stack mapping: Serilog request lines → keep (cheap), per-stage timings → histograms, EF commands → existing instrumentation (no custom spans needed), business milestones → Activity events. Costs: span volume (sample!), cardinality (tag discipline — same rules as log fields), collector ops (or vendor). Testing: InMemory exporters asserting spans/metrics in suites. Migration path: correlation ids first (today), OTel SDK next (activities auto-appear), custom meters last (business SLIs).
internalWorking: Activities stack in AsyncLocal (nested spans, parent linkage); samplers decide record/not at start (unsampled = near-zero cost); exporters batch over OTLP/gRPC. Meters aggregate in-process (lock-free counters) exporting deltas. W3C headers inject/extract at client/server instrumentation boundaries.
realWorldUsage: Microservice tracing, SLI dashboards (latency/error/burn), incident timelines, and performance baselines.
commonMistake: 100% sampling in prod (volume/cost explosion), high-cardinality tags (user ids as tags — cardinality bomb), no backend ownership (data nobody queries), and traces without metrics (pretty pictures, no alerts — metrics alert, traces explain).
technicalConversation: Ask what their p99 checkout latency is and where it goes — metrics answer in seconds; log-grep answers in hours (or never).
interviewFollowUp: Why sample by trace id, and what breaks when sampling is per-event instead?
keyTakeaway: One TraceId across logs/metrics/traces. Sample head-wise, tag leanly, alert on metrics.

questionText: How do hosted services (IHostedService/BackgroundService) manage lifetimes and shutdown?
shortAnswer: Hosted services are singletons: create scopes per unit of work (never inject scoped directly), honor CancellationToken (SIGTERM → 5s default shutdown), and make ExecuteAsync exception-safe (unhandled kills the host). Shutdown: stop accepting, drain in-flight, then exit.
detailedAnswer: Rules: singleton-only ctor deps (config, factories, channels — inject IServiceScopeFactory for DbContext/repos); per-iteration scopes (using var scope = scopes.CreateScope() — fresh DbContext per tick/message, no captive chains, no stale tracking); CancellationToken from ExecuteAsync (stoppingToken — pass everywhere: delays, HTTP, DB); exception discipline (try/catch per item — one poison message must not crash the host; fatal-only rethrow); startup ordering (no dependencies between hosted services — use health probes/readiness instead); shutdown sequence (StopAsync: signal completion (Channel.Writer.Complete), await drain with timeout, then return — host waits ShutdownTimeout, default 5s, then aborts). Patterns: timer loop (while + Task.Delay(interval, token)), queue consumer (await foreach ReadAllAsync), and cron-ish (schedule compute + delay, or Quartz/Hangfire for real schedules). Testing: extract logic to testable worker class (ExecuteAsync with fakes + cancelled token asserts prompt exit); silence in unrelated suites (RemoveAll<IHostedService>). Deployment: single-instance vs multi (leader election/leases for singleton jobs — outbox relay, schedulers).
internalWorking: Host starts services sequentially (StartAsync each, then Run loop); SIGTERM triggers ApplicationStopping → tokens cancel → StopAsync each (bounded by ShutdownTimeout) → dispose. Scoped creation per iteration keeps contexts short-lived (no growth, no staleness).
realWorldUsage: Outbox relays, queue consumers, cache warmers, scheduled syncs, and file watchers.
commonMistake: Scoped-in-hosted (captive — #1 worker bug), fire-and-forget tasks (unobserved exceptions crash), infinite retry without backoff/dead-letter (poison loops), and ignoring shutdown (lost in-flight work — drain first).
technicalConversation: Ask how their workers shut down on deploy — drain-then-exit (correct) versus abort-mid-batch (duplicates/loss) is the maturity check.
interviewFollowUp: Why must hosted-service constructors only take singletons, and what enforces it?
keyTakeaway: Singletons with scopes-per-unit, tokens everywhere, poison-proof loops, drain on shutdown.
